description: Ascetics who by ardent effort reach a concentration in which they recall up to a hundred thousand past lives, or many aeons, conclude that self and world are eternal. The text accepts the experience and rejects the conclusion: the Tathāgata knows where such grounds lead and what is beyond them.
One fallen from the non-percipient gods recalls in concentration only the arising of perception, 'but no further', and concludes he arose without cause.
In concentration some perceive the world as finite, others as infinite, and take the perception as proof.
Some take the pleasure of the senses, or the first, second, third or fourth absorption, for supreme nibbāna here and now.
(Jain report) Gosāla's fiery power burns two monks; hurled at Mahāvīra it circles him and enters Gosāla's own body, bringing fever and death within seven days.
(Jain report) Gosāla's claim that the soul of Udāyi Kuṇḍiyāyaṇa had entered his body as the seventh of a series of reanimations.
(Jain report) In his last fever Gosāla drinks, sings, dances and salutes; his followers interpret these as the eight finalities; on the seventh night he recovers his senses and repents.
(Jain report) By the eightfold Mahānimitta Gosāla foretells gain and loss, pleasure and pain, life and death.
Each of the six teachers claims to be an arahant with powers to win the sandalwood bowl; Piṇḍola flies up and takes it, and the Buddha forbids display of powers to lay people.
The Ājīvaka Upaka notices that the newly awakened Buddha's faculties are clear and his complexion bright, yet is not persuaded.
